mean: happening slowly, a little at a time
ex: After his knee surgery, Rohit's recovery was gradual: first a walk to the gate, then to the chai stall.
note: Opposite of sudden. The adverb 'gradually' is very useful: 'Prices gradually came down.'

mean: happening quickly when nobody expects it
ex: A sudden downpour sent the whole Dadar vegetable market running for plastic sheets.
note: The fixed phrase is 'all of a sudden', not 'all of sudden'. Sudden means unexpected; for speed alone, use 'quick' or 'rapid'.

mean: to get better, or to make something better
ex: Meera wants to improve her spoken English before the campus interviews in Pune.
note: No 'on' for things: 'improve your marks'. 'Improve on' means beat an earlier result: 'improve on last year's score'.

mean: to become smaller in number or amount, or to make it so
ex: Doctors expect the number of dengue cases to decrease once the monsoon ends.
note: Stress moves: the verb is dee-KREES, the noun is DEE-krees, just like increase. 'A decrease in sales'; 'a decrease of 10%'.

mean: lasting only for a short time, not for ever
ex: Metro work means a temporary diversion near Silk Board for the next two months.
note: Opposite of permanent. Stress the first syllable: TEM-puh-ruh-ree, not tem-po-RA-ry.

mean: to become less or worse; also, to politely say no
ex: Footfall at Kolkata's old single-screen cinemas began to decline once the multiplexes arrived.
note: Also means politely refuse: 'She declined the invitation' is softer than 'refused'. As a noun: 'a decline in sales'.

mean: to change slowly over a long time, usually into something more developed
ex: Film music continues to evolve, mixing Punjabi folk, Carnatic violin and electronic beats.
note: Evolve is slow and natural; for quick or forced change, use 'transform' or 'shift'. Not only animals: ideas, cities and languages evolve.

mean: firm and steady; not likely to change or fall
ex: After two days in the ICU, the doctor told the family that Nani's condition was finally stable.
note: Indian parents' 'stable job' means a secure one. Noun: stability. A horse's 'stable' is a different word with the same spelling.

mean: very fast; happening in a short time
ex: The rapid spread of UPI means even the sugarcane-juice seller near Charminar now takes payment by QR code.
note: More formal than 'fast'. Use it for change, growth or progress; for a person, say 'a fast runner', not 'a rapid runner'.

mean: lasting for ever or for a very long time
ex: After three years on contract, Shalini finally got a permanent post at the district hospital.
note: Indian forms ask for a 'permanent address' (your home town) and a 'present address'. Opposite: temporary.

mean: old-fashioned; not as good or useful as newer things
ex: The bank's outdated software crashed again, and the queue in Lucknow stretched out of the door.
note: Outdated things are still used but behind the times; obsolete things have mostly stopped being used. An old syllabus is outdated; a typewriter is obsolete.

mean: to bring back to life, use or strength
ex: Weavers in Chanderi hope that online orders will revive their struggling handloom trade.
note: Used for people (revive a patient), traditions, economies and old songs. Noun: revival.

mean: to slowly become worse
ex: Delhi's air quality began to deteriorate after Diwali, and schools shifted to online classes.
note: Say all five syllables: dih-TEER-ee-uh-rayt, not 'de-te-rate'. Usually things deteriorate on their own; we rarely say someone deteriorates something.

mean: to stop growing, moving or improving
ex: Without new skills, Farhan feared his career would stagnate in the same back-office job for years.
note: Comes from still, dirty water: a stagnant pond breeds mosquitoes. So it suggests going stale, not just taking a pause.

mean: a sudden, strong rise in amount or number
ex: There is always a surge in train bookings to Patna in the weeks before Chhath Puja.
note: Also a verb: 'The crowd surged forward.' Cab apps use 'surge pricing': fares jump when demand jumps.

mean: certain to happen; cannot be stopped or avoided
ex: With forty runs needed off two overs and one wicket left, defeat felt inevitable to the Ranchi crowd.
note: Stress the second syllable: in-EV-ih-tuh-bul. 'Accept the inevitable' means stop fighting what must happen.

mean: lasting only a short time; passing quickly
ex: The doctor said Kavya's dizziness was transient and would pass once she drank some ORS.
note: More formal than 'temporary'. A 'transient population' means people who keep moving in and out, like migrant workers or hostel students.

mean: no longer used because something newer has replaced it
ex: Pagers became obsolete in India almost as soon as cheap mobile phones arrived.
note: Stronger than outdated. 'Render something obsolete' means make it useless: 'Online forms rendered the queue obsolete.'

mean: never happened or seen before
ex: Chennai received unprecedented rainfall that December, and whole neighbourhoods went under water.
note: News channels overuse it to mean just 'big'. Use it only when something truly has no earlier example.

mean: lasting a very long time, or coming back again and again
ex: Waterlogging in Gurugram every monsoon has become a perennial problem.
note: From geography class: a perennial river like the Ganga flows all year, while a seasonal one dries up.

mean: the force or speed that keeps something moving or growing
ex: After two quick boundaries, the momentum shifted and the crowd at Eden Gardens sensed a comeback.
note: It is about keeping going once you have started. In physics, it is mass times velocity.

mean: cannot be changed back to how it was
ex: Years of untreated diabetes had caused irreversible damage to Mr Iyer's eyes.
note: Not 'unreversible'. Opposite: reversible.

mean: a state of constant change, where nothing is settled
ex: With the founders leaving and new investors arriving, the startup was in flux for months.
note: Almost always used as 'in flux' or 'in a state of flux'. In everyday speech, 'up in the air' is close.

mean: to wear away slowly, little by little
ex: Repeated paper leaks erode students' trust in the exam system.
note: Literally, rivers wear away land, as the Brahmaputra does to Majuli island. Figuratively, inflation erodes savings. Noun: erosion.

mean: lasting a very short time
ex: Rangoli is ephemeral art: hours of careful work, swept away by the next morning.
note: Literary. Use it for striking things that vanish (fame, trends, blossoms). For a short job or fix, plain 'temporary' is better.

mean: not wanting to change or act; staying the same out of habit
ex: Most people keep the same bank account for decades out of sheer inertia, not loyalty.
note: From physics: things stay still or keep moving unless pushed. In life, it means sticking with what is because change takes effort.
